prime.problem: Twenty-odd cards across seven courses are easy to read as a pile of separate topics. Without the map, a failure like the Tuesday run's false "all tests pass" gets filed under whichever card you read last, instead of under the owner whose record disagreed with the world.
prime.fits: The overview for course 0 and the map of the whole series. It ties the three map cards together (layers, boundary pairs, the forensics method) and routes you to courses 1–7 in order. It builds on the agent loop you already know.
expect: moment → owning layer → its record → course
the series path: 0, 1, then 2–4, then 5 and 6, then the capstone
levers grouped by what they change
prime.goal: For any agent failure, name the owning layer, the record to check against the world, and the course that treats it, and say which order to read the series in and why.

attend: Why does this overview use a lookup table instead of a formula, and what does each column of the table give you?
In the filled-in Tuesday row, which two owners failed, and why is "the model hallucinated" the wrong verdict?
Why can courses 2, 3 and 4 be read in any order, while course 5 must wait for course 4?
Which levers in the ranking would have caught the Tuesday run's false claim, and which only tell you where to put the fix?
Why do half of the series' 31 hours go to one paper?

must: Each layer owns one job and keeps one record → a failure is a disagreement between an owner's record and the world → name the moment, find the owner, check its record, and the fix lands in the right course
One word ("done", "session", "approved") hides two owners → a check on one gets read as a check on the other → split the word and keep a record per owner, or a green dashboard sits over a false claim
Forensics pins a release, fixes a boring task and adds a negative control → it shows where a claim can detach from the world → it can't say how often, so rates are left to evals and to the capstone
reference: the post URLs for each part of the map
the release numbers of his labs

compress.prompt: Card closed. Draw the series path with each course's owner and hours, then write the four columns of the ownership table and fill one row in for the Tuesday run's step 7.
checklist: 16 h of cards plus a 15 h paper, about 31 h in all
columns: the moment, the owning layer, its record, the course
step 7: layer 5 lost exit 1 from the working set; the transcript kept it; course 2
the false claim at step 9 was nobody's check: layer 9's job, course 4

retrieve.q: Explain what "ownership" means in this series and why Part 1 calls it, not the list of ten layers, the main idea.
answer: each layer owns one thing: the run, the working set, the capability, the side effect or the evidence
an owner keeps the record for its job
a failure then points at one owner whose record disagrees with the world
the list is a v1 that products slice differently; the ownership question survives that

retrieve.q: Walk the Tuesday run through the ownership table: for steps 6, 7 and 9 and the checker's re-run, give the owning layer, what its record says, and the course.
answer: step 6: execution (layer 7), pytest exit 1, a fact from the world
step 7: context (layer 5), working set says "tests passing" while the transcript (layer 2) keeps exit 1; course 2
step 9: the model writes the claim and the interface delivers it, unchecked
the checker's re-run: operator loop (layer 9), exit 1; course 4

retrieve.q: You have one week before the capstone. Courses 2, 3 and 6 remain unread. Which do you read, which do you skip, and what do you give up?
answer: the capstone needs 1, 2, 4 and 5, so read course 2 (compaction, the working set)
course 3 and course 6 are not prerequisites for the paper
skipping course 3 gives up authority and approval, including the injection question in the bank
skipping course 6 gives up the data-agent case study, not anything the paper measures

compare.q: The basics overview explains one coding agent through a token formula; this one explains the whole stack through an ownership table. What does each let you debug, and what would each miss about the Tuesday run?
answer: the token formula explains cost and context growth, and is the same whether pytest passed or failed
the ownership table explains which part failed and where the fix goes, and says nothing about cost
both put most fixes in the harness rather than the model
the Tuesday run needs both: compaction happened because of context growth, and it did harm because no owner checked the claim

compare.q: The ten-layers card stacks the layers around a request path; this overview turns them into a lookup and a reading order. What does the lookup add, and what does it hide that the picture shows?
answer: the lookup goes straight from a symptom to a record and a course
it adds the series' own mapping (9→4 for training, 1–10 for data agents), which is not his
the picture shows the shape: trust and operator layers wrapping the path, infrastructure under it
the lookup hides that some moments, like the final claim, have no owner on the request path at all

predict.q: A different run: the agent's push goes to the wrong branch because a stale session record from yesterday was loaded, and its final message correctly says "pushed to main". Commit to the owning layer, the record you check, the course, and whether this is a false success claim.
predict.answer: The control plane (layer 2) loaded the wrong session state, so check the session record and how it was keyed: course 1, owning the session. If the push really went to main as the message says, it is not a false success claim: the claim matches the world, and the failure is that the wrong action happened. That is why the ownership table starts from the moment, not from the final message; only some failures show up as a false claim.

apply.task: Take the last agent run of yours that went wrong. Write one row of the ownership table for it: the moment, the owning layer, the record you checked, what that record said vs what the world said, and the course you would open.
apply.done: You have one row with a layer number, a named record (a log, an exit code, a file hash, a receipt), the two values that disagree, and a course link.
apply.hint: If you can only say "the model got it wrong", look one step earlier: what did the working set contain on the call that went wrong?
